Lessons.Title: Multiplication as Equal Groups
ExplanationParagraphs: This is the ORIGINAL 2021 first-edition Illustrative Mathematics K–5 Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 9, Section B, addressing 3.OA.A and 3.OA.A.1. Learning focus: recognize and REPRESENT situations as concrete equal groups through picture graphs, dots, drawings and manipulatives, building toward multiplication. IMPORTANT TEACHING BOUNDARY: multiplication SYMBOLS or abstract multiplication expressions are NOT introduced in this lesson. Students should first describe grouping meaning. Teacher may provide twenty connecting cubes/counters per learner for original activities, plus MLR8 and representation supports. Timeline: 10-minute Number Talk, 15-minute original scaled-sign graph, 20-minute equal group situations, 10-minute synthesis, five-minute ORIGINAL source Jada bracelet Cool-down.

Warm-up — Number Talk: More Addition (10 minutes). The four 2021 source expressions are 40+35=75, 45+35=80, 45+36=81, 34+58=92. Learners mentally calculate each and discuss tens, ones and composing a ten, including relationships between the first three sums. Give a short think interval, invite alternative methods and teacher assessment of spoken reasoning. The four numeric checks are separate in the Edulytics student companion; numerical accuracy alone does not prove mental strategy.

Activity 1 — From Scaled Graphs to Equal Groups (15 minutes). Elena's graph 'Signs I Saw on the Way Home' uses key ONE SQUARE PICTURE = TWO ROAD SIGNS, with Stop signs 2 picture symbols (4 actual signs), Yield signs 1 (2), Speed limit signs 3 (6), Street signs 5 (10). The first original source subtask asks students to REPRESENT the six speed-limit signs as THREE DISTINCT groups, with TWO per group, using cubes, dots or a sketch. The second asks them to select the correct statement among THREE published possibilities: NOT 3 pictures each representing 1, NOT 2 pictures each representing 2, but YES 3 picture symbols each representing 2 speed limit signs (choice 2); explain WHY. The third asks how a diagram of FIVE groups of TWO dots can represent the ten street signs. Edulytics shows independently redrawn individual squares, NOT copied publisher art; teacher reviews constructions.

Activity 2 — Equal Group Situations (20 minutes). The source requires students to REPRESENT three distinct real-world situations with diagrams or physical objects rather than just write totals: FOUR people each wearing TWO shoes (four groups of two => eight shoes); TWO boxes with TEN markers in each (two equal groups of ten => twenty markers); THREE basketball teams with FIVE players on each (three equal groups of five => fifteen players). Pupils should point to group count, show objects per group, then explain why groups are equal and show a different representation if useful. Teachers support using at least twenty cubes/counters per student, conversation, and MLR8 as appropriate. The companion checks supporting totals 8,20,15 but its group diagrams and discussions remain explicitly teacher-reviewed.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes) BEFORE source Cool-down: compare the road-sign display and the three equal-group situations; ask what makes groups equal, why the graph symbol represents two real items, and how different drawings can represent the same total. Observe teacher-led partner conversations. The ORIGINAL first-edition five-minute Cool-down is named 'Represent Equal Groups': 'Jada has 3 bags. Each bag has 5 bracelets in it. Represent the situation.' The required source evidence is THREE SEPARATE groups with FIVE bracelets per group in a drawing or with counters. A bare total of fifteen is NOT sufficient and cannot receive an automatic pass. The first-party Edulytics stickers extra Cool-down is independently authored OPTIONAL practice, clearly separated from the publisher source task. Suggested teacher-led centers include Capture Squares Stage 4 and Five in a Row Stage 6.

KeyConcepts.Title: Concrete equal groups before symbolism
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equal-groups representation shows the same number of items in each of several distinct groups.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The lesson does not ask for multiplication symbols; students construct and explain groups with dots or blocks.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three speed-limit graph symbols each represent two signs: draw three groups each containing two sign counters.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scaled picture graph key
KeyConcepts.Definition: A picture key tells how many objects a single displayed picture stands for.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A key of two means every sign square must be interpreted as exactly TWO real signs.
KeyConcepts.Example: Stop 2 pictures=4 signs; Yield 1=2; Speed limit 3=6; Street 5=10.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number of groups versus objects per group
KeyConcepts.Definition: Representations distinguish how many separate groups are drawn from how many members are in each group.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State both meanings in words before calculating the combined total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four people each wearing two shoes: four equal groups, two shoes per group, eight shoes in all.

KeyConcepts.Title: Draw and interpret the same structure in different contexts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different contexts can share equal-group reasoning while retaining different group sizes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use counts and physical/drawn partitions matching each exact source situation.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two boxes of ten markers equals twenty; three basketball teams of five equals fifteen.

KeyConcepts.Title: Original publisher Cool-down is a construction
KeyConcepts.Definition: The 2021 Jada bracelet task evaluates a MODEL, not a scalar product.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Teacher checks three separate bags and five bracelets in EACH before considering totals. An integer alone never approves the source task.
KeyConcepts.Example: A correct drawing would have bag 1: five marks; bag 2: five; bag 3: five.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up: four mental sums
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 40+35, 45+35, 45+36 and 34+58 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use tens-and-ones decomposition or compensation, explaining a mental method.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each of the four source expressions has its own check; a teacher reviews the mental explanation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity1: source sign graph to equal-group drawing
WorkedExamples.Question: Three speed-limit pictures under a key of two signs each: represent them with groups and select which of three original statements is correct.
WorkedExamples.Method: Map one picture to one group of two real signs, without introducing multiplication expressions.
Steps: Count the three separate speed-limit pictures.
Read the key ONE picture stands for TWO signs.
Draw THREE separate groups, each showing TWO signs.
Count two, four, six; identify source statement TWO (three pictures each worth two signs).
Compare how five sets of two dots correspond to STREET signs.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Three groups of two = six speed-limit signs; source multiple-choice statement 2. Street signs form five groups of two = ten.
WorkedExamples.Check: 3 groups each of 2 are 6; 5 groups each of 2 are 10. Teacher reviews both source drawings and reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity2: three original equal-group contexts
WorkedExamples.Question: Show four people with two shoes each, two boxes of ten markers each and three basketball teams of five.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a physical or drawn group for each person, box and team.
Steps: Create FOUR groups with TWO shoe marks per group; count eight.
Create TWO groups with TEN marker dots per group; count twenty.
Create THREE groups with FIVE player marks per team; count fifteen.
Explain why each group contains the same quantity, and distinguish group count from total.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Four pairs of shoes = 8 shoes; two boxes of ten = 20 markers; three teams of five = 15 players.
WorkedExamples.Check: Correct numeric totals do not substitute for source-required group drawings and explanation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original 2021 Jada Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: Jada has THREE bags. Each bag has FIVE bracelets. Represent this situation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw the actual bags or physically separate counters into three equal groups of five.
Steps: Place exactly five bracelet marks inside the first bag.
Place exactly five in EACH of the second and third bags.
Explain how every bag has the same number and what the three groups represent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Three separate bags with five marks in each; optional total fifteen, but the drawing is the required source assessment.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher rubric: 3 groups, exactly 5 per group, distinguish bag count from bracelet count. A typed '15' alone is NOT enough.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Demanding a multiplication expression in this first equal-groups lesson.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 source deliberately reserves symbolic multiplication notation for a later lesson.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Represent with separate visible equal-sized groups, count and explain in words.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interpreting three speed-limit PICTURES as three speed-limit signs.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 picture graph key says each symbol represents two signs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw three groups of two and explain the six signs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing the original option that describes two symbols of two for the speed-limit bar.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: There are THREE source speed-limit picture symbols, not two.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Select original choice 2, meaning three symbols each worth two.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Showing eight shoes as one undifferentiated pile rather than four person-groups of two.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The aim is the meaning of equal groups, not just finding the product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw four distinct people/pairs, each with two shoe marks.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking Jada's publisher Cool-down complete from only the number 15.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original asks for a representation of three bags each with five bracelets.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require a teacher-reviewed three-by-five grouped drawing or manipulatives.

SummaryPoints: 2021 original purpose: introduction to concrete equal groups through scaled graph data, NOT multiplication expression notation.
Warm-up four original mental sums: 75,80,81,92 and explain related number-talk strategies.

Activity1 original picture graph, key one square=two signs, category real counts Stop4 Yield2 Speed limit6 Street10; three source parts involve drawing, correct statement choice2, and five groups of two.
Activity2 three original concrete cases: 4 people ×2 shoes, 2 boxes ×10 markers, 3 basketball teams ×5 players; require grouped drawings (not multiplication expression answers).
Lesson synthesis: explain what equal groups mean; original source Cool-down Jada three bags with five bracelets EACH requires a representation and teacher judgment.
Independent Edulytics sticker count task is OPTIONAL extra, not original Cool-down. Teacher-led Capture Squares Stage4 and Five in a Row Stage6 remain teacher facilitated; no original artwork copied.
